newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Solana outlines shape of new deal with Russia.
newsitem.headline: Solana outlines shape of new deal with Russia.

text.p: NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana proposed on Monday that Russia and the alliance station liaison officers in their respective military commands as a permanent feature of a new European security order.

Solana, who on Monday opened talks with Russian security supremo Alexander Lebed, says the proposal was one of many ideas to help build a close relationship between the former Cold War foes and reduce the chances of any future misunderstandings.
"NATO is working on ways to flesh out the substance of a new, permanent relationship with Russia," Solana wrote in an article published on Monday in the International Herald Tribune.
Solana and NATO capitals, keen to shift the emphasis of the talks with Lebed to areas of agreement, say the two sides must first build on the cooperation in the current peace mission in Bosnia.
"Why not build on this by having Russian officers permanently at NATO Supreme Command Headquarters and, reciprocally, NATO liaison officers at the Russian General Staff?," Solana added.

Alliance officials said Solana would detail the proposals, including suggestions for a NATO-Russia charter to govern all aspects of the new relationship, in the talks with Lebed, President Boris Yeltsin's security adviser.
Lebed, a former paratroop general, entered NATO's Brussels headquarters carrying what he said were new proposals to end tensions with Moscow over the alliance's plans to expand eastwards.
Solana said in several newspaper interviews on Monday, timed to coincide with Lebed's visit, that enlargement to take in new members from central and eastern Europe would go ahead.

He stressed these newly-democratic countries had a right to join "the Euro-Atlantic community to which they feel they legitimately belong", but said they would be joining a new NATO with a new mission spreading stability in Europe.
"If our vision of a new European security order is to be realized, that order must include Russia," Solana wrote.

U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry proposed at a NATO meeting in Norway late last month that the alliance "throw open its doors" to Russia to help convince its old enemy its intentions were not hostile.
Moscow opposes NATO's plans to take in new members from former communist Europe, particularly its former Warsaw Pact allies -- Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.

Western nations now say a limited expansion of the alliance is certain to begin next year but hope they can win Russian acquiescence by offering Moscow an upgraded relationship taking account of its weight in world affairs.
Perry's plan, creating standing arrangements for consultation and joint action between Russia and the alliance, would stop just short of full membership for Russia itself.
"Russia would have everything except Article 5," said one senior official referring to the key article committing NATO members to treat an attack on one as an attack on all of them.
NATO sources say they believe such a deal with Moscow would help solve the thorny problem of what to do with the former Soviet Baltic republics, Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania.
The three states bordering Russia all want NATO membership, but even their supporters accept it could only happen if the current European security architecture is completely redesigned.
"Welcoming new members into NATO does not require an enemy to justify it, nor is it directed against anyone," Solana said.
